content: The follow-up assessment revealed that only two patients were lost to follow-up. Regarding efficacy, the study did not identify any significant differences in PTSD symptoms at two or six months. A subgroup analysis based on age suggested that the intervention might be beneficial for children aged 7 to 11 in reducing depressive symptoms and behavioral problems. Kenardy and colleagues (2008) conducted a study to evaluate the efficacy of information booklets provided to participants within 72 hours of the initial trauma. These booklets aimed to normalize common stress reactions in children following trauma and offered basic self-help advice. The study was a cluster randomized trial involving two hospitals. One hospital provided the experimental intervention to 33 children (mean age 10 years), while the other hospital provided standard care to 70 children (mean age 10 years) admitted to pediatric units after accidental traumatic injuries. Outcomes were assessed at one and six months, but only 65 out of 103 children were evaluated at follow-up. The study found no efficacy of the experimental intervention in reducing post-trauma symptoms of intrusion and avoidance. Limitations included a high attrition rate and the use of only two clusters, which may have compromised the randomization process and the distribution of confounders. Cox and colleagues (2010) evaluated the efficacy of a web-based early intervention grounded in cognitive and resilience theories. They randomized 85 children and adolescents aged 7 to 16 years who had experienced unintentional injuries. The experimental group included 44 participants, while the control group consisted of 41 participants receiving standard care. Outcomes were assessed at 4–6 weeks and six months. At follow-up, data were available for 29 out of 44 children in the experimental group and 27 out of 41 in the control group. The completer analysis showed that children and adolescents in the experimental group reported improved anxiety levels. However, the intention-to-treat analysis did not demonstrate a positive effect of the intervention. The primary limitation of this study was the high attrition rate in both the experimental and control groups. A systematic review of evidence identified two studies investigating the efficacy of early psychological interventions based on cognitive-behavioral therapy (CBT) principles and two studies based on psycho-education principles. While the psycho-education studies did not yield positive findings, one of the CBT studies suggested that a four-session parent-child-focused intervention might be effective in reducing posttraumatic and anxiety scores. However, this study had limitations, including a small sample size (106 children) and a high attrition rate. The evidence remains inconclusive, and it is uncertain whether such interventions can prevent disorders, reduce symptom severity, or improve functioning after intervention. One randomized study on art therapy did not find any effect of the intervention, and two studies on debriefing yielded conflicting results. All studies had significant limitations. There is no systematic review of evidence on the potential harmful effects of early psychological interventions in children and adolescents with acute traumatic stress symptoms. The possibility of reducing acute traumatic stress symptoms and preventing PTSD is highly valued. However, many individuals with acute traumatic stress symptoms recover naturally over time without intervention. It may be prudent to wait 1–3 months to identify those who recover naturally and offer intervention only to those with persistent or worsening disabling symptoms, as recommended by NICE guidelines. Most primary healthcare staff in lowand middle-income countries lack extensive training in communication skills and basic emotional support. Additional training in early psychological interventions would require resources, including supervision. Delivering psychological interventions requires time, which is particularly challenging in resource-constrained settings, especially after mass events with numerous survivors. It would not be feasible to deliver CBT to all affected individuals. The limited available studies were conducted in industrialized countries. Based on the available evidence, no specific recommendation can be made regarding early psychological interventions (e.g., problem-solving counseling, relaxation, psycho-education, eye movement desensitization and reprocessing [EMDR], and CBT) for children and adolescents with acute traumatic stress symptoms associated with significant impairment in daily functioning. The quality of evidence is very low. However, WHO (2010) recommends offering access to psychological first aid to individuals recently exposed to potentially traumatic events. Therefore, psychological first aid should be considered for children and adolescents with acute traumatic stress symptoms and significant functional impairment within the first month after a potentially traumatic event. For adults with acute traumatic stress symptoms associated with significant functional impairment within the first month after a potentially traumatic event, pharmacological interventions (e.g., benzodiazepines and antidepressants) are commonly prescribed. However, there is no consensus on their effectiveness across clinical practice guidelines, making this an important area for further investigation. Symptoms of acute stress, such as intrusion, avoidance, hyperarousal, hyperventilation, dissociation, insomnia, and bedwetting in children, are frequently reported after exposure to potentially traumatic events. These symptoms are addressed in different evidence profiles within these guidelines. Pharmacological treatments, particularly benzodiazepines, are often used for acute distress symptoms, but their effectiveness remains uncertain.
